name: Luhu-Piru
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Collins, James T. 1983. The Historical Relationships of the Languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. (sealang PDF unreachable: expired certificate)

new_statements.quote: An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. For example, [moon / kind of fruit / tomorrow] Asilulu húlan e, ?úlul e, ráwa e; Luhu huláne, ulúle, rawá?e. Note too Asilulu pala?ekni [palá?ekən] recall him and Luhu pala?e?ena [pala?e?éna]. [...] This obligatory penultimate stress rule not only sometimes obscures cognate reflexes but in a few cases seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable.
new_statements.citation: Collins, James T. 1983. The historical relationships of the languages of Central Maluku, Indonesia. Pacific Linguistics D-47. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 82 (PDF page 92), Chapter IV, section 4 'Subgrouping of WPB, Part III: Luhu, Asilulu, Wakasihu and Batumerah', subsection 'Asilulu and Hoamoal'; continuation p. 82 bottom-83
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole word, including any suffix or (petrified) post-particle: when -e / -ne / -na etc. is added, stress moves right to stay penultimate (huláne, rawá?e, pala?e?éna). This is stated for all Hoamoal languages and exemplified with Luhu forms bearing acute accents; it contrasts with Asilulu, where stress stays on the root penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is called 'obligatory' and is said to drive deletion of antepenultimate vowels in some words (kallana 'wave', sumbeke 'shove', mandae 'male', p.83).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; the statement is in a comparative-historical monograph, illustrated with suffixed vs unsuffixed word forms (nouns with the permanent -e suffix, a verb with object suffix). The rule is phrased for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole (Luhu, Manipa, Kelang, Boano, Wakasihu), with Luhu as the illustrated language; Luhu is the author's own field language (informants incl. Hj. Abd. Rahman Payapo, p.136).
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is made for the Hoamoal subgroup of West Piru Bay (Luhu, Manipa mani1297, Kelang kela1256, Boano boan1242, Wakasihu waka1277) and exemplified with Luhu proper (the Luhu village variety, luhu1243); Piru (piru1241, bookkeeping) is treated by Collins (p.81) and the Holle list as a dialect of Luhu. The same p.82 sentence has already been used in this audit for boan1242; for Luhu it is first-hand (Collins's own field data with stress-marked Luhu forms), not second-order.

sources.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Lists Luhu (lcq, luhu1243) sources as Collins 1983, Stokhof 1982a, van Ekris 1864, 1865 (and Wahidah 2017 for Piru); comparative lexical data only, no Luhu stress statement (grep 'stress' hits concern other languages).

sources.citation: Stokhof, W.A.L. (ed.). 1982. Holle lists: vocabularies in languages of Indonesia, vol. 3/3: Central Moluccas: Seram (III), Haruku, Banda, Ambon (I). Pacific Linguistics D-49. Canberra: ANU. vi+219 pp. [Piru list no. 153, pp.1-9]
sources.note: Piru list (list 153) is a Dutch-era wordlist with acute/grave accents used as vowel-quality diacritics; note 1.2.1 says only 'Piroe and Loehoe speak the same language. Loehoe differs slightly in its pronunciation.' No stress statement for Piru/Luhu (the stress remarks on pp.11-12 belong to the Bonfia list, a different language).
